title: CP deployment regimens and Terraform hints
body:
Purpose:
This note captures a compact, operator-friendly runbook for first-time private control plane deployments and iterative upgrades. It focuses on practical Terraform module hints, state/secret handling, a safe upgrade/canary regimen, and node rotation patterns we’ve found effective in VPC and on-prem environments. This is intentionally operational (less design doc).

Scope and audience:
- Audience: infra engineers and platform operators performing initial bootstrap, periodic upgrades, or capacity rotations for the Private Control Plane (PCP).
- Scope: initial provisioning, terraform workflow conventions, scaling/rotation patterns, upgrade canaries and rollback play. Not a full network design doc; assumes customer network and firewall rules are provisioned per account onboarding checklist.

Preflight (quick checklist)
1) Access: Ensure you have org-level service account with KMS + bucket write, and a user account in customer VPN with SSH to bastion.
2) Secrets: Confirm KMS key ARN and vault path are shared with ops. Do NOT embed secrets in tfvars.
3) State: Confirm remote backend (S3/GCS) bucket, encryption, and DynamoDB/Cloud Storage lock table are available.
4) Observability: Prometheus scrape endpoints and temporary alert thresholds are enabled to avoid noisy alert storms during rollout.
5) Backups: Take a snapshot of etcd (if using k8s-managed etcd) and a copy of the tfstate file before any upgrade.

Network and DNS notes
- Split-horizon DNS: For on-prem we prefer per-customer private zone pointing controlplane.* -> internal LB. Verify resolver order on app hosts.
- MTU/Path MTU: Validate MTU and jumbo frame support across nodes (common failure for gRPC streams).
- Firewall rules: Allow health probes from load balancers and controlplane subnets. Document all ephemeral ports.

Terraform module / state conventions (practical hints)
- Module layout: keep infra modules (network/iam/storage) separate from cp modules (controlplane/agents). Apply infra first.
- Pin module versions in root module with required_providers and module source = git::...?ref=vX.Y.Z. Don’t rely on branch tips for production.
- Variables: keep sensitive values in environment-specific tfvars stored in vault, not in git. Example naming: cp-prod.us-east-1.tfvars.
- Backend: Use remote backend with state locking (S3 + DynamoDB or GCS + locks). Always terraform init with backend-config pointing at the correct bucket before applying.
- Workspaces: Avoid workspaces for long-lived prod environments; use separate state files per customer/env.
- Plan validation: Add a CI step that performs terraform plan and runs basic policy checks (sentinel/OPA) against the plan to catch drifts (e.g., accidental public IPs).

Secrets and KMS
- KMS usage: Envelope encrypt terraform secrets; store values in Vault or Kubernetes sealed secrets. Avoid storing KMS keys in tfstate in plaintext.
- Rotation: When rotating KMS keys, create a new key, add key to access policy, re-encrypt secrets, then remove old key after 30 days. Document key IDs in ticket.

Upgrade regimen (safe path)
Goal: minimize user impact by using stage -> canary -> bulk pattern.
1) Smoke stage (one node / small subset): apply controlplane changes to a single canary AZ or node pool. Target low-traffic times.
2) Health checks: confirm controlplane mats (latency, rpc errors, kv misses) are within baseline for at least 30 minutes.
3) Canary expansion: if canary OK, expand to 10–20% of capacity (additional node pool).
4) Monitor for 1h with elevated tracing and verbose metrics.
5) Full rollout: if stable, proceed with remaining nodes in waves (25% increments).
6) Post-rollout audit: run automated evals (synthetic traffic) and token-cost smoke to validate performance regression.

Rollback rules
- Always have plan output artifact (terraform plan --out=plan.tfplan) saved in associated ticket.
- Rollback by applying last-known-good infrastructure module ref or by restoring etcd (for k8s controlplane issues).
- If rollback requires tfstate restore, use state snapshot copy in backend bucket (naming convention: tfstate-backups/<env>/YYYYMMDD-HHMM).

Node rotation (drain and replace)
1) Mark node from LB pool as draining and stop routing new requests.
2) kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data <node> or provider-specific cordon/drain.
3) Wait for KV cache warmup: after new node comes up, warm KV caches by replaying a small set of synthetic requests that exercise common prefix workloads.
4) Monitor latency and error budget; if degraded, move next wave to pause.

Scaling strategies
- Horizontal: add identical node replicas with auto-scaler where possible. For on-prem, prefer capacity planning with pre-warmed standby nodes instead of instant autoscale.
- Vertical: increase instance type only for short-lived heavy queries and as a temporary mitigation—requires instance replacement.
- Cache-first: enable prefix/KV cache settings for large tails to reduce token compute during scale events.

Canary decisions and metrics
- Key signals: 95/99p latency, tail latency delta vs baseline, error rate (5xx/gRPC code), model quality regression (sampled prompts), token spend per request.
- Fast stop: if error rate > 0.5% absolute increase OR 99p latency increase > 50% for 10 minutes, abort rollout and rollback.

Common pitfalls and operator tips (lessons learned)
- Don’t change network or proxy config at the same time as runtime upgrades — isolates variables.
- Always test tfstate lock behavior in a staging account; lock misconfig causes concurrent apply corruption.
- When changing provider (e.g., upgrading AWS/GCP provider), pin provider versions and validate drift in staging. Provider upgrades are a separate canary.
- For airgapped installs: pre-stage all module artifacts and providers; do an offline terraform init with local mirror. Document checksums.

Commands and snippets (examples)
- Init with backend: terraform init -backend-config=\"bucket=cp-prod-tfstates\" -backend-config=\"region=us-east-1\"
- Plan and save: terraform plan -var-file=cp-prod.us-east-1.tfvars -out=plan-prod-20260310.tfplan
- Apply with lock/ticket: terraform apply \"plan-prod-20260310.tfplan\"
- Drain node: kubectl drain ip-10-0-1-23 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=120
- Restore state (example): gsutil cp gs://cp-prod-tfstates/backups/tfstate-20260228.json ./; terraform state replace-provider ... (followed by careful apply)

Post-upgrade checklist
- Verify controlplane health endpoints return 200 across AZs.
- Run synthetic workload that exercises typical customer prefixes and validate token/time cost is within +/-10% baseline.
- Confirm no new permission denials in audit logs and KMS key usage is expected.
- Update runbook and module refs in ticket and tag PRs that promoted modules.

Appendix: module versioning policy (short)
- Minor patches: allowed to auto-promote after green canary in non-prod.
- Minor features: require staging canary + one week observation.
- Major or provider changes: require two-stage canary and engineering signoff.

Open questions / next steps
- Add a CI job to auto-take tfstate snapshots before any prod apply.
- Create a small tool to replay synthetic prefix workloads to warm caches after node replacements.
- Formalize a traffic-split tool for on-prem LBs to ease canary traffic shifts.

If you’re the operator executing this: attach the ticket ID to all terraform artifacts and paste plan outputs into the runbook ticket for audit. When in doubt, pause and escalate to eng-private-deployments on-call before a full rollout.

Notes history:
- 2024-09-18: initial sketch (Asha)
- 2024-11-05: added KMS rotation steps (Miguel)
- 2025-06-21: incorporated tfstate backup naming convention (Priya)
- 2026-03-10: revised canary thresholds and added synthetic workload requirement (Samir)
